content.title: Artemis II mission couldn’t happen without Colorado. See state’s role
content.text: April 1, 2026, 5:02 a.m. MTAs the first launch of a manned lunar mission since 1972 nears, attention is focused on the launch site, the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.But Colorado has played a huge role in getting Artemis II to this point.Several critical components for the mission — from the crew capsule to communications systems to engines — were developed by companies in Colorado. Hundreds of jobs are directly supported by the program, and even more indirectly.And the work isn’t done with the launch. Some of Colorado’s aerospace companies will be ready to provide support if needed while the four-person crew goes on a 10-day mission that will sling them around the moon and back. Even more technology is being developed for future missions that will actually put people on the moon.What Colorado companies helped build Artemis II?Around 200 Colorado companies are involved in the Artemis program, including those that made some of the most important components of the rockets and spacecraft for Artemis II. They include:Lockheed Martin, which has based development of the Orion spacecraft — including the crew capsule — in Littleton since 2006, when it won the contract. Its presence has also been a boon for local suppliers.Centennial-based United Launch Alliance, which produced part of the propulsion system.Northrop Grumman’s team in Colorado Springs, which helped support the design and production of the solid rocket boosters it says will provide 75% of the thrust for launch.BAE Systems in Boulder, which developed the phased array antenna communications system used on the Orion.What is the Artemis II mission?Though no lunar landing is in store, the Artemis II mission will send a crew of four astronauts on a historic 10-day journey around the moon to test systems and hardware for future expeditions to the surface. The mission will also make history, with the astronauts traveling farther from Earth than any human has ever been in space. While traveling up to 6,000 miles above the lunar surface, the astronauts will see parts of the far side of the moon that not even the Apollo astronauts witnessed.At that distance, the moon will appear to the crew to be about the size of a basketball held at arm’s length, according to NASA.When does Artemis II launch? Time, dateNASA is planning an April 1 launch of the Artemis II mission, with a two-hour launch window opening at 4:24 p.m. MT. If the launch must be postponed, NASA has also said it has opportunities to launch April 2-6 and April 30.How do I watch Artemis II?It is likely many networks will carry the launch live, but NASA will begin streaming with live views and audio commentary starting at 5:45 a.m. MT on April 1 on NASA’s YouTube channel.Full coverage on NASA+ begins at 10:50 a.m. MT.Nate Trela covers trending news in Colorado and Utah for the USA TODAY Network. Eric Lagatta is the Space Connect reporter for the USA TODAY Network. Reach him at elagatta@usatodayco.com
